garment-steamers-handheld-2026.body:
Handheld garment steamers all look similar once you take the marketing photos away -- a wand, a water tank, a cord -- but the published spec sheets for three well-known models turn up real, measurable differences in exactly four numbers: wattage, tank capacity, heat-up time, and continuous steam time. The catch is that brands don't all publish that last one the same way, which matters more than it sounds like it should once you're standing in front of an empty tank mid-ironing. This guide walks through what each spec actually changes, then lines the three up side by side.

## Wattage tells you heat-up speed, not steam volume

Published wattage ranges from 1000W to nearly 1900W across handheld steamers, and the gap mostly buys you a faster heat-up, not more total steam over the life of a tank -- that's set by the tank size below. A higher-wattage unit gets to steaming sooner after you plug it in, which matters if you're steaming one shirt before you walk out the door. It matters less if you're working through a full load, where tank refills become the bigger time cost than the initial heat-up. It's also worth noting that wattage figures for the same model name sometimes disagree between retailer listings -- one unit in this category is listed as both 1550W and 1500W on the same page -- so a published number is a useful approximation rather than a guaranteed lab-tested figure.

## Water tank capacity is the real limiter on how long you can iron

Tank sizes in this category run small -- under 220 ml across every model we looked at -- which is the tradeoff for keeping a handheld steamer light enough to hold up and away from your body for several minutes at a time. A bigger tank means fewer trips back to the sink, but it also adds weight to a unit you're holding in one hand the whole time. None of these manufacturers publish how that weight changes as the tank empties, so treat the "full" weight on the spec sheet as the heaviest the unit will ever feel.

## Heat-up time adds up if you're steaming multiple garments

A 15-second difference in heat-up time looks trivial on a spec sheet, but if you're steaming five shirts back-to-back and the unit cools down between uses, that gap repeats every time. Heat-up specs are also measured from a cold start in a manufacturer's test lab; a unit that's already warm from recent use will be faster than its published number, and one that's sat unused for days may run slightly slower while it builds initial pressure.

## Continuous steam time isn't published the same way by every brand

This is the spec where shopping gets harder than it should be. Some brands publish a straightforward per-fill runtime in minutes. Others publish a steam output rate in grams per minute and leave you to divide it into the tank size yourself -- and at least one brand in this category publishes neither, listing only a maximum continuous-use safety limit that has nothing to do with how long a single tank actually lasts. If a listing doesn't give you a runtime number, assume it hasn't been measured for you and budget for refilling more often than the competitors that do publish one.

air-quality-monitors-2026.body:
Air quality monitors look like a single product category until you compare what they actually measure -- some units track one pollutant with heavily documented lab-grade precision, others track seven with far less detail published about accuracy. Four specs explain most of the real difference: which pollutants a unit covers, what sensor technology does the measuring, how you read the results, and how it's powered. This guide walks through each one, then compares three monitors that take meaningfully different approaches to the same basic job.

## Pollutants measured is the first fork in the road

Some monitors are single-purpose instruments: one sensor, one number, documented in detail. Others bundle five to seven pollutants -- particulates, CO2, VOCs, sometimes radon -- onto one device and one screen. Broader coverage isn't automatically better; it usually means less documentation per sensor and a device built around convenience rather than any single reading's precision. Radon in particular is worth flagging on its own: it's the one pollutant here that only one of these three monitors measures at all, and it's not something the other two are quietly estimating -- they simply don't track it.

## Sensor type determines how much you can trust a single number

The most useful spec on a monitor's page isn't the pollutant list, it's the sensor technology and its stated accuracy range, when the manufacturer publishes one. An NDIR (non-dispersive infrared) CO2 sensor with a published accuracy of plus or minus a fixed ppm value and a percentage of the reading is a spec you can actually evaluate and compare between products. A manufacturer that lists "CO2 sensing" with no sensor model or accuracy figure is asking you to trust the number without the means to check it. This isn't just a budget-vs-premium split, either -- in this category, the most fully-specified sensor info came from the single-pollutant device, not the one with the most sensors.

## Display format changes whether you need a phone to read it

E-ink displays trade color and detail for low power draw and a screen you can read in direct sunlight without a glare problem -- a meaningful reason a device can run for years on a couple of AA batteries instead of needing a daily charge. Color touchscreens pack more simultaneous readings into one glance and make historical trends easier to page through, at the cost of real power draw, which is exactly where the rechargeable-battery runtimes in this category get short. A status-glow indicator (a colored ring or light, separate from the main display) adds a readable-from-across-the-room signal that neither pure e-ink nor a touchscreen gives you on their own.

## Power source sets how much maintenance the monitor needs

Replaceable AA batteries are the lowest-maintenance option by far when the rated life is measured in years rather than hours, since you're not tracking a charge cycle at all. Built-in rechargeable batteries push runtime down into single-digit hours on some units, which in practice means leaving the monitor on USB power most of the time rather than treating it as cordless. One monitor in this category does double duty when plugged in, acting as a WiFi relay for other sensors from the same brand elsewhere in the home -- worth knowing if you're planning to add more than one unit later, since that can change which model you want to plug in permanently versus run on battery.

smart-body-composition-scales-2026.body:
Smart body composition scales all run the same basic trick -- a weak electrical current and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to estimate body fat, muscle, and water on top of a plain weight reading -- but three published spec sheets from well-known brands show real differences in how many metrics they report, how a reading gets from the scale to your phone, how many people in a household the scale can tell apart, and what keeps it running day to day.

## Metrics tracked ranges wider than the core BIA numbers suggest

Every scale in this category reports weight, body fat percentage, muscle mass, and water percentage at minimum, since that's what a single BIA sensor pair produces. Where they differ is how many additional numbers get derived from that same reading and surfaced in the app -- bone mass, BMI, and other calculated stats stacked on top of the same raw measurement. A higher metric count on a spec sheet isn't a sign of extra hardware in most cases; it's the manufacturer's software deriving more numbers from the same underlying impedance reading, so treat the count as a feature-richness spec rather than a precision spec.

## Connectivity decides whether a weigh-in syncs itself or waits on your phone

A WiFi-connected scale pushes each reading to the app on its own, which means your phone doesn't need to be in the room, let alone unlocked, for the data to log. A Bluetooth-only scale needs your phone nearby and the app open (or at least backgrounded and paired) to capture a reading in real time -- step on a Bluetooth-only scale with your phone in another room and you may not get a synced number at all. This is a bigger day-to-day difference than it looks on paper, especially for a scale that's going to live in a bathroom where phones don't usually live too.

## Max users stored determines whether the scale actually knows who's standing on it

Multi-user support means the scale (or more precisely, the app) tries to recognize who just stepped on based on weight and impedance patterns and log the reading to the right profile automatically. The published limits vary by brand and, in at least one case we found, by which page on the brand's own site you're reading -- one official page for a model promised unlimited users while a separate FAQ from the same company capped "many models" at 16. If exact profile limits matter for your household, the safest move is cross-checking the number against the scale's own app listing rather than trusting a single marketing page.

## Power source is a bigger factor than it looks for a WiFi scale specifically

All three scales here run on AAA batteries rather than a rechargeable cell, which keeps the scale from ever needing a charging cable but means battery life is entirely about how often the scale talks to your network. A WiFi scale wakes up its radio and pushes a sync on every single use, which draws more power than a Bluetooth-only scale that mostly stays idle between weigh-ins -- and the two WiFi-capable scales in this comparison don't even agree with themselves on expected battery life, with one brand listing two different numbers on two of its own pages. Don't assume a quoted battery-life figure is the floor; treat it as one brand's average case.
